## Course Syllabus: Programming for Data Science

Based on the official syllabus of the College of Technology, National Economics University (version dated 17 June 2025). The original syllabus is attached at the end of this lesson.

### General information

| Item | Details |
|---|---|
| Course | Programming for Data Science |
| Responsible unit | College of Technology – National Economics University |
| Date offered | February 2026 |
| Credits and workload | 2 credits – 30 hours of studying: 20 hours of class contact and 10 hours of independent study |
| Course duration | 4 weeks |
| Pre-requisites | Principles of Programming |
| Website | https://nct.neu.edu.vn/ |

### Course Description

This foundational course introduces learners to Python, the most widely used programming language in data science and software development. By the end of this course, learners will be able to:

- Understand and apply core programming constructs: variables, data types, control flow, functions, and object-oriented programming.
- Work proficiently with essential Python libraries such as NumPy and Pandas in Jupyter Notebooks.
- Access and retrieve data from the web using APIs and Python scraping tools such as BeautifulSoup.

### Learning Outcomes

**Knowledge.** Upon successful completion of the course, students will gain a foundational understanding of programming in Python, including core constructs such as variables, data types, control flow, functions, and object-oriented programming. They will understand how Python is used in modern data science and software development, and how it enables efficient data manipulation and analysis. Students will also develop knowledge of essential data science libraries, specifically NumPy and Pandas, and how to utilize Jupyter Notebooks.

**Skills.** Students will be able to write structured Python programs using both procedural and object-oriented approaches. They will work proficiently with numerical and tabular data using NumPy and Pandas, and perform data processing tasks interactively in Jupyter Notebooks. Furthermore, students will acquire practical skills in accessing web-based data sources through RESTful APIs and conducting basic web scraping using BeautifulSoup.

### Course Content and How to Study on the Platform

| Module | Syllabus content | On the platform |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Fundamentals of Python Programming | Introduction to variables, data types, operators, control flow (if statements, loops), functions, and basic object-oriented programming. | 11 short video units of 3–6 minutes, each with in-video questions and a quiz; 4 review lessons; a capstone practice |
| 2. Data Manipulation with NumPy and Pandas | Working with arrays and DataFrames, including data cleaning, transformation, aggregation, and exploratory data analysis using Jupyter Notebooks. | 4 readings with runnable code, each with a quiz; a lab on data cleaning and exploration |
| 3. Accessing and Collecting Web Data | Retrieving data via RESTful APIs, extracting JSON data, and performing basic web scraping using BeautifulSoup. | 2 readings with code, each with a quiz; a data collection lab; an end-of-course knowledge check |

### Teaching Method

The course will utilize a blended learning approach that combines the following methods to ensure both theoretical understanding and practical application:

- **Face-to-face teaching:** Instructor-led lectures and live coding sessions to explain core programming concepts and demonstrate Python tools in action.
- **Group discussion:** Collaborative activities and peer interaction to explore data science problems and share coding solutions.
- **Case-based assignments:** Practical exercises and mini-projects based on real-world data science scenarios to reinforce programming and data analysis skills.
- **Individual and group presentations:** Opportunities for learners to present their solutions, explain code logic, and receive feedback from instructors and peers.
- **Self-study:** Guided readings, online tutorials, and practice notebooks to deepen understanding and promote independent learning.

### Assessment

1. Group Project and Presentation (40%)
2. Final Exam (60%)

The quizzes, assignments and end-of-course knowledge check on the platform help you practice and assess yourself. They do not replace the two assessment components above.

### Required Literature

- McKinney, W. (2022). *Python for Data Analysis: Data Wrangling with Pandas, NumPy, and Jupyter* (3rd ed.). O'Reilly Media.
- Mitchell, R. (2018). *Web Scraping with Python: Collecting Data from the Modern Web* (2nd ed.). O'Reilly Media.

items.body:
## 1.1 Python and Basic Syntax

**After this unit you will:** choose the right Python version, and write a piece of code with no basic syntax errors.

### Key points

- Always use **Python 3** — Python 2 reached end of life in 2020.
- Python is **case-sensitive**: `age`, `Age`, `AGE` are three different names.
- Blocks are defined by **indentation** (4 spaces per PEP 8); the line that opens a block ends with `:`.
- A single-line comment starts with `#`.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.1 — Basic Syntax
quizzes.description: 7 questions on versions, case sensitivity and indentation.

questions.prompt: In Python, age, Age and AGE are three different variables.
questions.explanation: True — Python is case-sensitive.

questions.prompt: What does Python use to define the scope of a block of statements?
questions.explanation: Indentation (the PEP 8 convention is 4 spaces). The line that opens a block, such as if or for, ends with a colon.

options.label: A semicolon at the end of the line

questions.prompt: Which character starts a single-line comment?
questions.explanation: The # character — everything from there to the end of the line is ignored by Python.

questions.prompt:
When you run the following code, which error does Python raise?

score = 5
if score > 3:
print("high")
questions.explanation: The print line belongs inside the if block but is not indented, so Python raises an IndentationError (an indented block is expected after a line ending with a colon). Fix it by indenting the print line with 4 spaces. All the variables here are defined and the comparison 5 > 3 is valid, so there is no NameError or TypeError.

options.label: TypeError: cannot compare the number 5 with the number 3
NameError: the variable score is not defined
No error, the program prints the word high
IndentationError: an indented block is needed after the if line

questions.prompt: The statement Print("hello") (with a capital P) still runs normally because Python does not distinguish between uppercase and lowercase letters.
questions.explanation: False — Python is case-sensitive. The built-in function is called print (lowercase); Print is a different name that has not been defined, so Python raises a NameError.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

total = 3
# total = total + 10
print(total)
questions.explanation: Everything from the # character to the end of the line is a comment and is ignored by Python, so 10 is never added to total and it stays 3.

options.label: An error, because the comment line has invalid syntax

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

n = 5
if n > 10:
    print("A")
    print("B")
print("C")
questions.explanation: The two lines print("A") and print("B") are indented, so they belong to the if block; since 5 > 10 is false, the whole block is skipped. The line print("C") is not indented, so it is outside the if and always runs. Indentation is what decides which lines belong to a block.

options.label: A, B, then C (each letter on its own line)

questions.prompt: Which Python version should you use for new work?
questions.explanation: Always use Python 3. Python 2 reached end of life in 2020 and no longer receives updates.

options.label: Python 2, because it is more stable

items.body:
## 1.2 Variables, Input and Output

**After this unit you will:** declare variables following the conventions, print results neatly and read data from the user.

### Key points

- Naming: variables and functions use `snake_case`, constants use `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`, classes use `PascalCase`.
- `del x` deletes the name `x`; using `x` afterwards causes a `NameError`.
- `print(*objects, sep=' ', end='\n')` — `sep` is what is inserted between values, `end` is what is inserted at the end.
- f-string: `f"{score:.2f}"` prints 2 decimal places.
- **`input()` always returns a string** — to do calculations you must convert the type: `int(input(...))`.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.2 — Variables and Input/Output
quizzes.description: 8 questions on input, del, f-strings and print.

questions.prompt: Which type does the input() function return?
questions.explanation: input() always returns a string (str), even when the user types 42. To use it as a number you must convert the type, for example int(input(...)). If you forget this step, "5" + 1 raises a TypeError.

options.label: int if the user types a number, otherwise str
It depends on the variable receiving the value

questions.prompt: After running x = 5, then del x, then print(x), Python raises a NameError.
questions.explanation: True — del x deletes the name x, so using x afterwards is a NameError.

questions.prompt: With score = 9.456, what does f"{score:.2f}" give?
questions.explanation: .2f means a floating-point number with 2 decimal places, with rounding: 9.456 becomes 9.46.

questions.prompt: What does print(1, 2, 3, sep='*') print?
questions.explanation: sep is the string inserted between values (a single space by default). With sep='*' we get 1*2*3.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

print("Hello", "world", sep="-", end="!")
print("Python")
questions.explanation: sep is the string inserted between values (here "-"), so the first output is Hello-world; end is the string appended at the end of the output (here "!" instead of the default newline character), so the next print continues immediately after it: Hello-world!Python.

options.label: Hello-world! then Python on the next line

questions.prompt: Given score = 9 (an integer). Which way prints exactly the line Score: 9?
questions.explanation: An f-string needs the letter f before the opening quote for {score} to be replaced with the value 9. Without the f, Python prints {score} literally. Concatenating a string with a number using + raises a TypeError because you cannot add a str and an int, and writing two values side by side without a comma is a SyntaxError.

questions.prompt: According to the PEP 8 convention, which roles are the three names MAX_USERS, user_count and UserProfile, respectively, best suited for?
questions.explanation: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (MAX_USERS) is for constants, snake_case (user_count) is for variables and functions, and PascalCase (UserProfile) is for class names. Every other order assigns a naming style to the wrong role.

questions.prompt:
The user types 5 when running the following code, and the program prints 10.

x = input()
print(x * 2)
questions.explanation: False — input() always returns a string, so x is "5" and "5" * 2 is string repetition, giving "55". To get 10 you must convert the type: int(input()) * 2.

questions.prompt: According to the PEP 8 convention, what naming style should a constant such as a maximum value use?
questions.explanation: Constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, for example MAX_SIZE or PI. Variables and functions use snake_case, while class names use PascalCase.

options.label: Starting with an underscore, for example _max_size

lessons.description: Arithmetic and assignment operators, comparison and logic, in/is, and operator precedence.

items.body:
## 1.3 Operators and Expressions

**After this unit you will:** read and write expressions correctly, and know which operator runs first.

### Key points

- `/` always gives a float; `//` is floor division (rounds down); `%` is the remainder; `**` is exponentiation.
- `n % 2 == 0` checks whether n is even.
- `==` compares **values**; `is` checks whether two names point to the **same object**, and is commonly used to check for `None`.
- Precedence from highest to lowest: `**`, then `* / % //`, then `+ -`, then comparisons, then `is`/`in`, and finally `not and or`.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.3 — Operators
quizzes.description: 7 questions on `is`, exponentiation and precedence.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, what is the is operator mainly used for?
questions.explanation: == compares values, while is checks whether two names point to the same object. That is why is is mainly used to check for None (x is None); to compare values, use ==.

options.label: Comparing whether two numbers or two strings are equal
Checking whether an element is in a list
Checking whether a variable is None
Comparing whether one number is greater or less than another

questions.prompt: What is the value of the expression 2 ** 10?
questions.explanation: ** is exponentiation: 2 to the power of 10 = 1024.

questions.prompt: Arrange the following operator groups in order of precedence from HIGHEST to LOWEST, exactly as in the table in the lecture.
questions.explanation: Exponentiation (**) first, then multiplication and division (* / % //), then addition and subtraction, then comparison, then is / in, and finally not, and, or (lowest).

options.label: is, is not, in, not in

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

print(2 + 3 * 4 ** 2)
questions.explanation: Exponentiation (**) has the highest precedence: 4 ** 2 = 16; then multiplication: 3 * 16 = 48; finally addition: 2 + 48 = 50. If you added first or multiplied first, ignoring precedence, you would get 80, 196 or 400.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

print(-7 // 2)
questions.explanation: // is floor division, meaning it rounds DOWN: -7 / 2 = -3.5, and rounding down gives -4 (not -3). Only truncating the decimal part, as in int(-3.5), gives -3.

questions.prompt: For a positive integer n, which expression is True if and only if n is odd?
questions.explanation: n % 2 is the remainder when dividing by 2: odd numbers leave a remainder of 1. n // 2 == 1 is only true for n = 2 or 3, n % 2 == 0 checks for even numbers, and n / 2 == 1 is only true for n = 2.

questions.prompt: The expression not True or True evaluates to True, because not is evaluated before or.
questions.explanation: True — not has higher precedence than and, or: (not True) or True = False or True = True. Only if or were evaluated first would not (True or True) give False.

questions.prompt: What are the results of print(7 // 2) and print(7 % 2), respectively?
questions.explanation: // is floor division (rounds down), so 7 // 2 = 3; % is the remainder, so 7 % 2 = 1. It is 7 / 2 that gives 3.5, because / always returns a float.

lessons.title: 1.4 Numbers, Booleans and Strings
lessons.description: Numeric and boolean types, truthiness, and how to index, slice and use string methods.

items.body:
## 1.4 Numbers, Booleans and Strings

**After this unit you will:** correctly predict whether a value is truthy or falsy, and slice a string at the right positions.

### Key points

- Falsy: `False None 0 0.0 '' [] () {} set()`. Everything else is truthy — even the string `"False"`.
- `True + True` equals 2 (booleans are numbers).
- Strings are indexed from 0; the slice `s[a:b]` **stops just before b**; `s[::-1]` reverses.
- Strings are **immutable**: you cannot change individual characters.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.4 — Numbers and Strings
quizzes.description: 8 questions on slicing, string operators, immutability and booleans.

questions.prompt: With s = 'Hello World!', what does the expression s[2:5] give?
questions.explanation: Indexes start at 0: s[2]='l', s[3]='l', s[4]='o'. The slice stops just BEFORE index 5, so it takes positions 2, 3, 4 → 'llo'.

questions.prompt: What does "ab" * 3 give?
questions.explanation: Multiplying a string by an integer repeats it: "ab" * 3 = "ababab".

questions.prompt: Strings in Python are immutable — you cannot assign s[0] = 'J' to change the first character.
questions.explanation: True — to change it you must create a new string (for example with replace or string concatenation).

questions.prompt: What is the value of True + True?
questions.explanation: bool is a subclass of int: True equals 1, so True + True = 2.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

data = [0]
if data:
    print("yes")
else:
    print("empty")
questions.explanation: The truthiness of a list depends on whether the list is empty, not on the values inside it. [0] has one element, so it is truthy even though that element is 0; only an empty list [] is falsy.

options.label: An error, because 0 is not a valid condition

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

s = "Python"
print(s[::-1])
questions.explanation: The slice s[::-1] has a step of -1, so it walks through the string from the end to the start, i.e. it reverses the string: "Python" becomes "nohtyP".

questions.prompt: Given s = 'hello'. Which way creates the string 'Hello' (capitalizing the first letter)?
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, so you must create a new string: "H" + s[1:] joins the letter H with the rest. s[0] = "H" raises a TypeError; s.upper() does not modify s but returns a new string HELLO (all uppercase); s.replace(0, "H") also fails because replace takes strings, not positions.

questions.prompt: With s = 'Python' (6 characters), the statement s[6] raises an IndexError because valid indexes run from 0 to 5.
questions.explanation: True — indexes start at 0, so the last character is s[5]. s[6] goes past the end of the string and causes an IndexError. (Slices, however, do not raise an error when they go out of range: s[2:99] still works.)

questions.prompt: What does bool("False") return?
questions.explanation: Every non-empty string is truthy, regardless of its content — so bool("False") is True. Only the empty string '' is falsy.

options.label: False, because the content is the word False

lessons.title: 1.5 List
lessons.description: Create, index, add and remove elements, copy and sort lists.

items.body:
## 1.5 List

**After this unit you will:** work with lists without falling into the copying trap.

### Key points

- A list is ordered, **mutable**, and allows duplicates: `nums[0] = 99`.
- Adding/removing: `append`, `insert`, `extend`, `remove`, `pop`, `del`, `clear`.
- **`b = a` does not make a copy** — both names point to the same list. For a real copy, use `a.copy()`.
- `a.sort()` sorts in place; `sorted(a)` returns a new list.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.5 — List
quizzes.description: 7 questions on slicing, mutability, and sorting.

questions.prompt: With nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], what does nums[1:3] return?
questions.explanation: The slice takes positions 1 and 2 (stopping before 3): [2, 3].

questions.prompt: After nums[0] = 99, the list nums is modified in place.
questions.explanation: True — a list is mutable, unlike a string or a tuple.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a.sort() and sorted(a)?
questions.explanation: a.sort() sorts the list a itself (in place) and returns None; sorted(a) leaves a unchanged and returns a new sorted list.

options.label: sorted(a) sorts in place; a.sort() returns a new list
a.sort() sorts in place; sorted(a) returns a new list
a.sort() can only be used on strings

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

a = [1, 2]
a.append([3, 4])
b = [1, 2]
b.extend([3, 4])
print(len(a), len(b))
questions.explanation: append adds EXACTLY ONE element to the end — here that element is the whole list [3, 4] — so a = [1, 2, [3, 4]] has 3 elements. extend adds each element of the list passed in, so b = [1, 2, 3, 4] has 4 elements.

questions.prompt:
A student wants top to be the list of scores sorted in ascending order, but after the following code top is None. Why?

scores = [7, 9, 6]
top = scores.sort()
questions.explanation: scores.sort() sorts the list scores itself (in place) and returns None, so assigning its result to top gives None. To get a new sorted list while keeping scores unchanged, use top = sorted(scores).

options.label: sort() sorts in place and returns None; to get a new list you must use sorted()
sort() returns an unsorted copy of the list
You must declare top = [] before calling sort()
sort() only works on lists of strings; on a list of numbers it returns None

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

nums = [10, 20, 30, 20]
nums.remove(20)
last = nums.pop()
print(nums, last)
questions.explanation: remove(20) removes only the FIRST occurrence of 20, leaving [10, 30, 20]. pop() with no argument removes and returns the last element, 20, leaving [10, 30].

questions.prompt: With a = [1, 2, 3] and b = a.copy(), the expression a == b gives True while a is b gives False.
questions.explanation: True — copy() creates a new list with the same contents: == compares values so it is True, while is checks whether both names refer to the same object so it is False. With b = a (no copy), both are True.

questions.prompt: Given a = [1, 2, 3], then b = a is run followed by b.append(4). What is a now?
questions.explanation: b = a does NOT create a copy — a and b are two names for the same list, so adding 4 through b is visible through a as well: [1, 2, 3, 4]. For an independent copy, use b = a.copy().

options.label: Raises an error because a list is immutable

lessons.title: 1.6 Tuple, Set, Dictionary, and Type Conversion
lessons.description: The remaining three collection types and how to convert between data types.

items.body:
## 1.6 Tuple, Set, Dictionary, and Type Conversion

**After this unit you will:** choose the right collection type for each problem.

### Key points

| Type | Ordered | Mutable | Duplicates |
|---|---|---|---|
| List `[]` | Yes | Yes | Allowed |
| Tuple `()` | Yes | No | Allowed |
| Set `{}` | No | Yes | Not allowed |
| Dict `{k: v}` | Yes | Yes | Keys are unique |

- A one-element tuple needs a comma: `(50,)`.
- A dictionary can be nested: `students["s1"]["name"]`.
- `int(3.99)` is 3 — `int()` truncates the decimal part rather than rounding.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.6 — Tuple, Set, Dictionary
quizzes.description: 8 questions on tuples, nested dictionaries, and type conversion.

questions.prompt: With t = ('physics', 'chemistry', 1997), the statement t[0] = 'maths' raises a TypeError.
questions.explanation: True — a tuple is immutable. To "change" it, convert it to a list, edit it, then convert it back.

questions.prompt: Which of these creates a tuple with only ONE element, the number 50?
questions.explanation: The comma is what makes a tuple: (50,). (50) is just the number 50 in parentheses.

questions.prompt: Given students = {"s1": {"name": "Anna", "scores": [8, 9, 7]}}. What does students["s1"]["name"] return?
questions.explanation: Go level by level: students["s1"] is the inner dictionary, then ["name"] retrieves the value "Anna".

questions.prompt: What value does int(3.99) return?
questions.explanation: int() truncates the decimal part rather than rounding (truncates, does not round), so int(3.99) = 3. To round, use round().

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

students = {"s1": {"name": "Anna", "scores": [8, 9]}}
students["s1"]["scores"].append(7)
print(students["s1"]["scores"])
questions.explanation: students["s1"]["scores"] goes through two levels of dictionary and returns the list [8, 9] stored inside; append modifies that list in place (a list is mutable), so printing gives [8, 9, 7].

options.label: Raises AttributeError because a dictionary has no append

questions.prompt:
What happens when the following code is run?

codes = ["A1", "B2", "A1", "C3", "B2"]
unique = set(codes)
print(len(unique), unique[0])
questions.explanation: A set is unordered, so it cannot be indexed: unique[0] raises TypeError (the object does not support indexing). Because print evaluates its arguments before printing anything, the error occurs first and nothing is printed, not even len(unique) = 3. If you need a position, convert to a list: list(unique)[0].

options.label: Prints 3 and then raises an error on the second value
Raises TypeError because a set is unordered and cannot be indexed

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

print(int("12") + int(3.99))
questions.explanation: int("12") converts the string to the number 12; int(3.99) truncates the decimal part rather than rounding, giving 3. The sum 12 + 3 = 15. Only if int rounded would the result be 16.

options.label: Raises TypeError because it mixes strings and numbers

questions.prompt: The dictionary {"a": 1, "a": 2} raises no error; it keeps only one key "a" with the value 2.
questions.explanation: True — dictionary keys are unique; when a key is repeated, the later value overwrites the earlier one and Python raises no error.

questions.prompt: What does print({1, 2, 3, 2, 1}) output?
questions.explanation: A set does not allow duplicate elements, so repeated values are dropped: {1, 2, 3}.

options.label: Raises an error because of duplicate elements

lessons.title: 1.7 Branching with if / elif / else
lessons.description: Control program flow with if, elif, else, nested if statements, and pass.

items.body:
## 1.7 Branching with if / elif / else

**After this unit you will:** write chains of conditions and correctly predict which branch will run.

### Key points

- Python checks from top to bottom and runs the **first branch whose condition is true**; the remaining branches are skipped.
- `else` belongs to the nearest `if` at the same indentation level.
- `pass` is a placeholder statement that avoids a syntax error when a block has not been written yet.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.7 — Branching
quizzes.description: 7 questions on evaluation order, pass, and else.

questions.prompt: In an if / elif / else chain, what happens when several conditions are true?
questions.explanation: Only the first branch whose condition is true runs; Python skips every branch after it.

options.label: Only the last true branch runs
Only the first true branch runs

questions.prompt: What is the pass statement used for?
questions.explanation: pass is a placeholder statement — it does nothing, but it lets an empty block avoid a syntax error.

options.label: Holding the place of a block that has not been written yet, avoiding a syntax error

questions.prompt: else belongs to the nearest if statement at the same indentation level.
questions.explanation: True — the indentation level decides which if an else pairs with when if statements are nested.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

x = 15
if x > 10:
    print("A")
if x > 5:
    print("B")
else:
    print("C")
questions.explanation: These are TWO independent if statements, not one if/elif chain. The first if is true so it prints A; then Python still checks the second if: 15 > 5 is true so it prints B, and the else (which belongs to the second if) is skipped. If the second line were written as elif, only A would be printed.

questions.prompt:
A student wants scores of 90 or above to get grade A, but with score = 95 the following code prints C. What is the cause?

score = 95
if score >= 70:
    grade = "C"
elif score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
else:
    grade = "F"
print(grade)
questions.explanation: Python runs the first branch whose condition is true and skips every branch after it. score >= 70 is a broad condition that is already true for 95, so the score >= 90 branch is never evaluated. The narrowest condition (>= 90) must come first, with the broader conditions after it.

options.label: The else branch runs because 95 satisfies none of the conditions
The condition score >= 70 comes first and is already true, so the later branches are skipped
95 is an integer, so it cannot be compared with 90
The line elif score >= 90 has a syntax error so it is skipped

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

age = 20
has_id = False
if age >= 18:
    if has_id:
        print("enter")
    else:
        print("show ID")
else:
    print("too young")
questions.explanation: age >= 18 is true so the outer block runs. Inside it, the else is indented at the same level as if has_id, so it belongs to if has_id: since has_id is False, this else runs and prints "show ID". The outermost else (at the same level as if age) is the too-young branch and does not run.

questions.prompt: The line if x = 5: is a valid way to check whether x equals 5.
questions.explanation: False — = is the assignment operator and cannot be used as a condition (SyntaxError). To compare, use ==: if x == 5:.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

score = 78
if score >= 90:
    grade = 'A'
elif score >= 80:
    grade = 'B'
elif score >= 70:
    grade = 'C'
else:
    grade = 'F'
print(grade)
questions.explanation: Python checks from top to bottom and runs the first branch whose condition is true; the remaining branches are skipped. 78 is not ≥ 90 and not ≥ 80, but it is ≥ 70, so grade = 'C'.

## 1.8 for and while Loops

**After this unit you will:** choose the right kind of loop and predict exactly how many times it runs.

### Key points

- `range(start, end, step)` **stops just before `end`**: `range(2, 6)` gives 2, 3, 4, 5.
- `break` exits the loop; `continue` skips the current iteration.
- An `else` after a loop runs only if the loop was **not** ended by `break`.
- Use `for` when the number of iterations is known in advance; use `while` to repeat until a condition becomes false.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.8 — Loops
quizzes.description: 8 questions on while, else, break/continue, and range with a step.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

i = 1
while i < 6:
    print(i)
    i += 1
questions.explanation: The while loop runs as long as i < 6 is true. i goes from 1 to 5; when i = 6 the condition is false so the loop stops, and 6 is not printed.

questions.prompt: The else block attached to a for loop still runs when the loop is exited with break.
questions.explanation: False — a loop's else runs only when the loop finishes normally, without a break.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between break and continue?
questions.explanation: break exits the loop entirely; continue only skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next one.

options.label: break skips the current iteration; continue exits the loop
break exits the loop; continue skips the current iteration
The two statements are the same
break can only be used in while

questions.prompt: Which sequence does range(2, 20, 3) generate?
questions.explanation: It starts at 2, adds 3 each time, and stops before 20: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

count = 0
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(4):
        count += 1
print(count)
questions.explanation: The outer loop runs 3 times (i = 0, 1, 2); on each pass the inner loop runs all 4 times (j = 0..3). The total number of count += 1 executions is 3 × 4 = 12, not 3 + 4.

questions.prompt:
The following code runs forever. Why?

i = 0
while i < 3:
    print(i)
questions.explanation: The loop body never changes i, so i is always 0 and the condition i < 3 is always true: the loop prints 0 forever. The condition variable must be updated, for example by adding the line i += 1 at the end of the loop body.

options.label: The variable i does not change in the loop body, so the condition i < 3 is always true
0 < 3 is not a valid condition in a while loop
A while loop always needs a break statement to stop
The print statement decreases the value of i on each iteration

questions.prompt: In which case should you use a while loop instead of a for loop?
questions.explanation: while is suited to repeating until a condition stops being true when the number of iterations is not known in advance, such as asking for a password again until it is correct. The other three cases all have a known number of iterations or a collection of elements to traverse, so they use for.

options.label: Going through each character of a given string to count the vowels
Asking for a password again until it is correct, with the number of attempts unknown in advance
Adding up all the elements of a given list of scores
Printing the numbers from 1 to 10 in order

questions.prompt: The loop for i in range(5) gives i the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in turn.
questions.explanation: False — range(5) starts at 0 and stops just before 5, so i takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (exactly 5 iterations). To get 1..5 you must write range(1, 6).

questions.prompt: Which sequence of numbers does the loop for i in range(2, 6): print(i) print?
questions.explanation: range(start, end) stops just BEFORE end, so range(2, 6) generates 2, 3, 4, 5 — not 6.

items.body:
## 1.9 Functions

**After this unit you will:** package a task into a reusable function and understand where variables live.

### Key points

- A **parameter** is the name in the definition; an **argument** is the value passed at call time.
- Default parameter: `def power(base, exp=2)`.
- `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a **tuple**; `**kwargs` collects keyword arguments into a **dict**.
- `lambda x: x ** 2` is a one-line anonymous function.
- Assigning inside a function creates a new **local** variable; to change an outer variable you must declare it `global`.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.9 — Functions
quizzes.description: 8 questions on variable scope, *args, lambda, and parameters.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

x = 10

def change():
    x = 99

change()
print(x)
questions.explanation: Assigning x = 99 inside the function creates a new local variable also named x; it does not touch the outer x, so print(x) still prints 10. To change the outer variable you must declare global x inside the function.

questions.prompt: In the definition def total(*numbers), when you call total(1, 2, 3), what is numbers?
questions.explanation: *args collects the extra positional arguments into a tuple, so numbers = (1, 2, 3). It is **kwargs that collects keyword arguments into a dictionary.

options.label: Only the first value, which is 1

questions.prompt: Given square = lambda x: x ** 2, what is the value of square(5)?
questions.explanation: lambda x: x ** 2 is a squaring function: 5 ** 2 = 25.

questions.prompt: In def area(width, height) and the call area(3, 4), what are 3 and 4 called?
questions.explanation: width and height are parameters (names in the definition); 3 and 4 are arguments (values passed at call time).

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

def f(*args, **kwargs):
    return args, kwargs

print(f(1, 2, x=3))
questions.explanation: *args collects the extra positional arguments (1, 2) into a tuple; **kwargs collects the keyword arguments (x=3) into a dictionary {'x': 3}. The function returns both as a two-element tuple.

questions.prompt:
The following code prints None instead of 5. Why?

def add(a, b):
    total = a + b

result = add(2, 3)
print(result)
questions.explanation: A function without a return statement returns None by default; total is only a local variable and disappears when the function ends. Fix it by adding return a + b (or return total).

options.label: You must declare global result before calling add
total is a local variable, so it is deleted and replaced by 0
Parameters a and b have no default values
The function has no return statement, so it returns None by default

questions.prompt:
Given the function below, what does the call power(exp=3, base=2) return?

def power(base, exp=2):
    return base ** exp
questions.explanation: Keyword arguments are matched by parameter name, not by order: base = 2, exp = 3, so 2 ** 3 = 8. Only if they were matched by position (base = 3, exp = 2) would the result be 9.

options.label: Raises TypeError because keyword arguments must be in order

questions.prompt: With a global variable count = 0, simply writing count += 1 inside a function increases the outer count without any further declaration.
questions.explanation: False — count += 1 is an assignment, so Python treats count as a local variable of the function; since it has no value yet, it raises UnboundLocalError. To change the outer variable you must declare global count inside the function (or, better: pass it in and return it).

questions.prompt: Given def power(base, exp=2): return base ** exp, what does the call power(3) return?
questions.explanation: exp has a default value of 2, so when exp is not passed, 2 is used: 3 ** 2 = 9. Only power(3, 3) gives 27.

options.label: Raises an error because the argument exp is missing

items.body:
## 1.10 Classes and Objects

**After this unit you will:** be able to write a simple class and create multiple objects from it.

### Key points

- A **class** is a blueprint; an **object** (instance) is a concrete entity created from the class.
- `__init__` is the constructor; `self` is the object that is calling the method.
- An **instance attribute** (`self.name`) belongs to each individual object; a **class attribute** (`Student.university`) is shared by all objects.
- Python interprets `anna.status()` as `Student.status(anna)`.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.10 — Classes and Objects
quizzes.description: 7 questions on instance attributes, the constructor, and self.

questions.prompt: There are two objects anna = Student("Anna", 3.8) and binh = Student("Binh", 2.9). After running anna.name = "Anna Nguyen", what is the value of binh.name?
questions.explanation: name is an instance attribute — each object keeps its own copy, so changing anna.name does not affect binh. Only a class attribute (such as Student.university) is shared by all objects.

options.label: Raises an error because attributes cannot be reassigned

questions.prompt: What is the name of the special method that is called automatically when a new object is created from a class (the constructor)?
questions.explanation: __init__ is the constructor of a class in Python; self is the first parameter and refers to the object being created.

questions.prompt: How does Python actually interpret the call anna.status()?
questions.explanation: Python passes the object as the first argument: anna.status() is equivalent to Student.status(anna). That is why the method has a self parameter.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

class Student:
    university = "Tech"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

a = Student("An")
b = Student("Binh")
Student.university = "NEU"
print(a.university, b.university)
questions.explanation: university is a class attribute shared by all objects: a and b do not keep their own copies but read directly from the class. When Student.university is changed, both see the new value NEU.

questions.prompt:
What happens when you run the following code?

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        name = name

d = Dog("Rex")
print(d.name)
questions.explanation: name = name only assigns the parameter to a local variable of the same name; it does not create an attribute of the object. Without self., d has no name attribute, so d.name raises AttributeError. The correct form is self.name = name.

options.label: TypeError, because Dog("Rex") is missing an argument
AttributeError, because name = name only creates a local variable
Prints None because the attribute has no value yet
Prints Rex because the name parameter was stored in the object

questions.prompt:
What error does Python raise when you run the following code?

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, gpa):
        self.name = name
        self.gpa = gpa

an = Student("An")
questions.explanation: When an object is created, Python automatically passes the new object into the self parameter; you do not write it out. The call Student("An") supplies only name and is missing gpa, so it raises TypeError: missing 1 required positional argument: 'gpa'.

options.label: AttributeError because there is no gpa attribute yet
No error; gpa automatically becomes None
TypeError because the gpa argument is missing; self is passed by Python automatically
TypeError because the self argument is missing

questions.prompt: When does Python run the __init__ method of a class?
questions.explanation: __init__ is called automatically exactly once for EACH object, right when the object is created (Student("An", 3.8)); you do not call it by hand. Defining the class does not create any object, so __init__ has not run yet, and using the object afterwards (calling methods, assigning attributes) does not run it again either.

options.label: Only when you call it by hand after creating the object
Every time you call any method of the object
Exactly once, as soon as the class is defined
Automatically as soon as a new object is created from the class

questions.prompt: In object-oriented programming, how do a class and an object differ?
questions.explanation: A class is a blueprint that describes what data an object has and what it can do; an object (instance) is a concrete entity created from that class.

options.label: A class is a concrete entity, an object is a blueprint
A class is a blueprint, an object is a concrete entity created from it
A class only contains functions, an object only contains variables

items.body:
## 1.11 Inheritance, Encapsulation, and Polymorphism

**After this unit you will:** be able to tell apart the three most commonly confused concepts of OOP.

### Key points

| Concept | Meaning | Example in this lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Inheritance** | A child class reuses everything from its parent class and can add to it or override it (an "is-a" relationship) | `class Dog(Animal)` |
| **Encapsulation** | Protecting internal data from being modified arbitrarily | `self.__balance` + `deposit()` |
| **Polymorphism** | The same method name, different behavior depending on the object | `speak()` of Dog, Cat, Cow |

Use `super()` to **extend** a parent class's method rather than replace it entirely.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1.11 — The Three Pillars of OOP
quizzes.description: 7 questions distinguishing inheritance, polymorphism, and the use of super().

questions.prompt: Dog, Cat, and Cow all have a speak() method, but each class produces a different result (Woof!, Meow!, Moo!). Which concept does the loop for a in animals: print(a.name, 'says', a.speak()) illustrate?
questions.explanation: The same method name with different behavior depending on the object is polymorphism. Inheritance is a child class reusing its parent class's code; encapsulation is protecting the internal data of an object.

questions.prompt: Given class Dog(Animal), which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Dog inherits from Animal: an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog is an Animal); Dog reuses everything from Animal and can add or override (override) its own parts, for example speak().

options.label: The two classes are independent and unrelated
Dog is the child class and inherits the attributes and methods of Animal
Dog is an object of Animal

questions.prompt: When should you use super() in a child class?
questions.explanation: super() lets you call the parent class's method in order to extend it, rather than replace it entirely.

options.label: To delete the parent class's method
To extend the parent class's method rather than replace it entirely

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

class Animal:
    def speak(self):
        return "..."

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return "Meow"

class Fish(Animal):
    pass

print(Cat().speak(), Fish().speak())
questions.explanation: Cat overrides speak(), so it returns "Meow". Fish defines nothing extra, so it inherits Animal's speak() unchanged and returns "...". This is inheritance (Fish) combined with overriding (Cat).

options.label: Raises AttributeError because Fish has no speak()

questions.prompt:
What happens when you run the following code?

class Account:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__balance = 100

acc = Account()
print(acc.__balance)
questions.explanation: An attribute that starts with two underscores is renamed by Python inside the class (to _Account__balance), so accessing acc.__balance directly from outside raises AttributeError. The intent of encapsulation is to force outside code to go through methods such as deposit().

options.label: Raises TypeError because __balance is a constant
Raises AttributeError because __balance cannot be accessed directly from outside the class

questions.prompt: Among the following class pairs, which one makes sense for inheritance?
questions.explanation: Inheritance models an "is-a" relationship: a Car is a Vehicle, so class Car(Vehicle) makes sense. An Engine is a PART of a Car (a "has-a" relationship), not a Car; this relationship should be represented with an attribute (car.engine), not with inheritance.

options.label: class Student(Car), because both have a name attribute
class Engine(Car), because an Engine is part of a Car
class Car(Vehicle), because a Car is a Vehicle
class Car(Engine), because a Car has an Engine

questions.prompt: If a child class overrides speak() without calling super().speak(), then when speak() is called on an object of the child class, the parent class's speak() method will not run.
questions.explanation: True — overriding completely replaces the parent class's method. To still run the parent class's part (extend rather than replace), you must call super().speak() inside.

questions.prompt: In the BankAccount class, the balance is stored in self.__balance and can only be changed through deposit() (which rejects non-positive amounts). What is the purpose of encapsulation here?
questions.explanation: Encapsulation protects the internal data of an object from being modified arbitrarily: every change must go through a method that validates it.

options.label: To protect internal data from being modified arbitrarily
To let a child class reuse the parent class's code
To use the same method name for multiple behaviors
To make the program run faster

## Variables, Data Types, and Operators

**Review lesson.** A summary table of the *variables, data types, and operators* part of Module 1, for quick lookup and self-checking after studying units **1.2 → 1.6**. If anything is still unclear, go back to the corresponding unit and rewatch the video.

### Data types

| Type | Example | Ordered | Mutable | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `int`, `float` | `42`, `3.14` | — | — | `/` always gives a `float`, `//` is floor division |
| `str` | `'Python'` | Yes | **No** | Indexing starts at 0, slice `s[a:b]` stops before `b` |
| `bool` | `True`, `False` | — | — | `True + True` equals 2 |
| `list` | `[1, 2, 3]` | Yes | Yes | `b = a` does **not** copy; use `a.copy()` |
| `tuple` | `(1, 2)` | Yes | **No** | A single element needs a comma: `(50,)` |
| `set` | `{1, 2, 3}` | No | Yes | Duplicate elements are not allowed |
| `dict` | `{"a": 1}` | Yes | Yes | Keys are unique; `d.get(k, default)` does not raise an error when the key is missing |

### Operators and precedence

From highest to lowest: `**` → `* / % //` → `+ -` → comparison → `is`, `in` → `not and or`.

### Four easily confused points

- `input()` always returns a **string**; to do arithmetic you must convert the type: `int(input(...))`.
- `==` compares **values**, `is` checks for **the same object** (commonly used for `None`).
- *Falsy* values: `False None 0 0.0 '' [] () {} set()`; the string `"False"` is still truthy.
- `int(3.99)` is 3 — `int()` truncates the decimal part, it does not round.

### Key points

- Variables/functions use `snake_case`, constants use `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`, classes use `PascalCase`.
- **Mutable** types (list, set, dict) and **immutable** types (str, tuple) determine how they behave when assigned and passed into functions.

quizzes.title: Review — Variables, Data Types, and Operators
quizzes.description: 6 review questions with explanations.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

print(10 // 3, 10 % 3, 2 ** 3)
questions.explanation: // is floor division (10 // 3 = 3), % is the remainder (10 % 3 = 1), ** is exponentiation (2 ** 3 = 8).

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

x = [1, 2, 3]
y = x
y.append(4)
print(x)
questions.explanation: y = x does not create a copy: x and y are two names for the same list, so appending 4 through y is also visible through x. To get an independent copy you must use x.copy().

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

s = 'Python'
print(s[1:4], s[-1])
questions.explanation: s[1:4] takes positions 1, 2, 3 (stopping before 4): 'yth'. s[-1] is the last character: 'n'. print separates the values with a space.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
print(d.get("c", 0), len(d))
questions.explanation: d.get("c", 0) returns the default value 0 when the key does not exist (it does not raise an error like d["c"] does); len(d) is the number of keys: 2.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

a = [1]
b = [1]
print(a == b, a is b)
questions.explanation: == compares VALUES: the two lists have the same content [1], so True. is checks whether they are the same OBJECT: a and b are two separate lists (each [] creates a new list), so False.

questions.prompt: You need to store full names by student ID and look up a name as soon as you know the ID. Which data type is the most suitable?
questions.explanation: A dictionary stores key–value pairs, where the key is the student ID (unique) and the value is the full name, looked up with names[student_id]. A set only holds single elements and is unordered, a tuple is a fixed sequence, and a long string concatenating all the names cannot be looked up by ID.

options.label: dictionary: student ID as the key, full name as the value
a set of full names: a set cannot store the accompanying ID
a single tuple (ID, name) for the whole class
a long string joining all IDs and names with commas

items.body:
## Control Flow: Conditionals and Loops

**Review lesson.** A summary of the *conditionals and loops* part of Module 1, for quick reference and self-checking after units **1.7 → 1.8**.

### Conditionals

```python
if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 80:
    grade = "B"
else:
    grade = "C"
```

- Python checks from top to bottom and runs **the first branch whose condition is true**, skipping the remaining branches.
- `else` belongs to the nearest `if` at the same indentation level; `pass` is a placeholder for a block that has not been written yet.

### Loops

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Repeat a known number of times, or go through each element | `for` |
| Repeat until the condition becomes false | `while` |
| Exit the loop completely | `break` |
| Skip the rest of the current iteration | `continue` |

- `range(start, end, step)` **stops right before `end`**: `range(2, 6)` gives 2, 3, 4, 5.
- An `else` attached to a loop runs only when the loop is **not** ended by a `break`.
- In a `while` loop, remember to update the condition variable; otherwise the loop runs forever.

### Remember

- Indentation determines the code block; being off by one level means wrong logic.
- Count the number of iterations of a loop by tracing the first few iterations by hand on paper.

quizzes.title: Review — Conditionals and Loops
quizzes.description: 6 review questions with explanations.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

for i in range(5):
    if i % 2 == 0:
        continue
    print(i)
questions.explanation: continue skips the current iteration when i is even (0, 2, 4), so only the odd numbers 1 and 3 are printed.

questions.prompt:
What number does the following code print?

n = 10
c = 0
while n > 1:
    n //= 2
    c += 1
print(c)
questions.explanation: n takes the values 10 → 5 → 2 → 1 (it stops because n > 1 is false): the loop runs 3 times, so c = 3.

questions.prompt:
What number does the following code print?

total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total += i
print(total)
questions.explanation: range(1, 5) generates 1, 2, 3, 4 (stopping before 5): the sum = 10.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

for x in [1, 2, 3]:
    if x == 5:
        break
else:
    print('done')
questions.explanation: The else of a loop runs when the loop finishes normally (without a break). No element equals 5, so there is no break, and 'done' is printed.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print? (end="" makes consecutive prints join together)

for n in range(1, 8):
    if n % 3 == 0:
        print("F", end="")
    elif n % 2 == 0:
        print("E", end="")
    else:
        print(n, end="")
questions.explanation: For each n, Python runs the first branch whose condition is true: n = 6 is divisible by 3, so the F branch runs first and the E branch is skipped even though 6 is also even. Result: 1, E (n=2), F (n=3), E (n=4), 5, F (n=6), 7, i.e. 1EFE5F7.

questions.prompt:
How does a while True: loop (the condition is always true) end? Example:

n = 0
while True:
    n += 1
    if n == 3:
        break
print(n)
questions.explanation: Because the condition True is never false, the loop stops only when a break (or a return, or an error) occurs inside it. Here n increases to 3, then break runs and exits the loop, so 3 is printed. Without a break, the loop runs forever.

options.label: Only when a break (or return) is hit inside the loop body
After exactly one iteration, just like an if statement
When Python sees the first variable in the loop body change value
Never, even if the loop body contains a break

**Review lesson.** A summary of the *functions* part of Module 1, for quick reference and self-checking after unit **1.9**.

### Syntax and parameters

```python
def area(width, height=1, *extras, **options):
    return width * height
```

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Parameter** | A name in the function definition (`width`, `height`) |
| **Argument** | A value passed at call time (`area(3, 4)`) |
| Default parameter | `height=1` — used when no argument is passed |
| `*args` | Collects extra positional arguments into a **tuple** |
| `**kwargs` | Collects keyword arguments into a **dict** |
| `return a, b` | Returns multiple values (actually a tuple) |
| `lambda x: x ** 2` | A one-line anonymous function, often used as `key=` for `sorted` |

### Variable scope

- Assigning inside a function creates a new **local** variable and does not change a variable with the same name outside.
- To change an outer variable, you must declare `global x` inside the function (use sparingly; prefer passing values in and using `return`).

### Remember

- A function should do **one thing** and have a name that says what it does.
- Place parameters that have default values **after** the required parameters.

## Basic Object-Oriented Programming

**Review lesson.** A summary of the *object-oriented programming* part of Module 1, for quick reference and self-checking after units **1.10 → 1.11**.

### Class and object

```python
class Student:
    university = "Tech Institute"        # class attribute: shared by all objects

    def __init__(self, name, gpa):       # constructor
        self.name = name                 # instance attribute: separate for each object
        self.gpa = gpa

    def status(self):
        return "Honours" if self.gpa >= 3.5 else "Regular"
```

- A **class** is a blueprint; an **object** (instance) is a concrete entity: `anna = Student("Anna", 3.8)`.
- `self` is the object that is calling the method; `anna.status()` is equivalent to `Student.status(anna)`.
- Changing `anna.name` does not affect other objects; changing `Student.university` affects every object.

### The three pillars

| Concept | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Inheritance** | A subclass reuses its parent class (an "is-a" relationship); use `super()` to extend | `class Dog(Animal)` |
| **Encapsulation** | Protect internal data, and change it only through methods that validate | `self.__balance` + `deposit()` |
| **Polymorphism** | The same method name behaves differently depending on the object | `speak()` of Dog, Cat |

### Remember

- Distinguish **instance attributes** (`self.x`) from **shared attributes** (assigned at class level).
- `isinstance(obj, ParentClass)` is `True` even for objects of a subclass.

items.body:
## NumPy Arrays

**After this lesson you will be able to:** create and access NumPy arrays, compute on whole arrays without loops, and understand why arrays are more compact and faster than lists.

### 1. Why NumPy

Python lists are very flexible but slow with large amounts of data, because every element is a separate object. A NumPy array (`ndarray`) stores numbers of the **same type** contiguously in memory, so computations are fast and the syntax is concise. Pandas is built on NumPy: understanding arrays first makes DataFrames much easier.

### 2. Creating arrays

```python
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2))    # [0 2 4 6 8]  (like range: stops before 10)
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))   # [0.   0.25 0.5  0.75 1.  ]  (5 evenly spaced points, including both endpoints)
print(np.zeros((2, 3)))       # array of all zeros with 2 rows x 3 columns
print(np.ones(3))             # [1. 1. 1.]
```

Every array has three frequently used attributes: `shape` (the size of each dimension), `ndim` (the number of dimensions) and `dtype` (the common data type).

```python
m = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])
print(m.shape)   # (2, 3)
print(m.ndim)    # 2
print(np.array([1, 2.5]).dtype)   # float64  (one float makes the whole array float)
print(np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4).shape)   # (3, 4)
```

### 3. Indexing and slicing

Indices start at 0. For a 2-dimensional array, write `m[row, column]`; the `:` symbol means "all".

```python
print(m[1, 2])    # 6   (row 1, column 2)
print(m[:, 1])    # [2 5]   (all of column 1)
print(m[0])       # [1 2 3] (all of row 0)
```

Slicing `a[i:j]` stops right **before** `j`, just like with lists.

### 4. Whole-array computation (vectorization)

Operations apply to **each element** without needing `for`:

```python
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a * 2)      # [2 4 6]
print(a + 10)     # [11 12 13]  ← broadcasting: the number 10 is "stretched" to match the array
print([1, 2, 3] * 2)   # [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]  ← with a list, * repeats the list, NOT element-wise multiplication
```

**Broadcasting** lets you add or multiply an array by a number (or by a smaller array with a compatible shape) without writing a loop.

### 5. Filtering with a condition (boolean mask)

```python
b = np.array([5, 1, 4, 2, 3])
print(b > 2)      # [ True False  True False  True]
print(b[b > 2])   # [5 4 3]   (keeps the elements satisfying the condition)
```

### 6. Aggregate functions and the `axis` parameter

```python
print(m.sum())           # 21
print(m.mean())          # 3.5
print(m.sum(axis=0))     # [5 7 9]   (sum down the rows → one sum per column)
print(m.sum(axis=1))     # [ 6 15]   (sum across the columns → one sum per row)
```

Memory tip: `axis=0` means "collapse the rows" (leaving one value for each column); `axis=1` means "collapse the columns".

### Common mistakes

- Confusing `*` on lists with `*` on NumPy arrays (see section 4).
- Confusing `axis=0` with `axis=1`.
- Thinking a slice includes the last index.

### Remember

- NumPy arrays: same type, fast, element-wise computation.
- `shape`, `ndim` and `dtype` describe an array.
- Filtering with a condition: `a[a > 2]`.
- `axis=0` gives a result per column, `axis=1` gives a result per row.

### Reference

McKinney, W. (2022). *Python for Data Analysis: Data Wrangling with Pandas, NumPy, and Jupyter* (3rd ed.). O'Reilly Media.

## Pandas DataFrames

**After this lesson you will be able to:** create a DataFrame, inspect its structure, select rows and columns correctly with `loc` and `iloc`, and filter data by condition.

### 1. DataFrame and Series

A **DataFrame** is a table of data with rows and columns (like an Excel sheet); each column is a **Series** (a labeled sequence of values). Real data is usually loaded from a file: `pd.read_csv("grades.csv")`.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name":  ["An", "Binh", "Chi", "Dung", "Em"],
    "major": ["IT", "IT", "Econ", "Econ", "IT"],
    "score": [8.5, 7.0, 9.0, 6.5, 7.5],
})
print(df.shape)     # (5, 3)  → 5 rows, 3 columns
print(df.head(2))   # first 2 rows
df.info()           # column names, data types, number of non-null values
print(df.describe())   # descriptive statistics for the numeric columns
```

Reading from a CSV file (the example below uses a string instead of a file so you can run it right away):

```python
import io
csv = "name,score\nAn,8.5\nBinh,7\n"
small = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv))
print(small.shape)   # (2, 2)
```

### 2. Selecting columns

```python
df["score"]          # one column → a Series
df[["name", "score"]]  # several columns (two pairs of brackets) → a DataFrame
df[["score"]]        # one column, but wrapped in a list → still a DataFrame
```

The double brackets `[[...]]` mean "pass in a list of column names", so the result is always a DataFrame.

### 3. Selecting rows: `loc` and `iloc`

- `loc` selects by **label** (row/column name), and its slices **include** the end label.
- `iloc` selects by **position** (index number starting from 0), and its slices stop **before** the end position, like a list.

```python
print(df.loc[0:2, "name"].tolist())    # ['An', 'Binh', 'Chi']   ← includes label 2
print(df.iloc[0:2]["name"].tolist())   # ['An', 'Binh']          ← stops before position 2

by_name = df.set_index("name")         # use the name column as the row labels
print(by_name.loc["Chi", "score"])     # 9.0   (by label "Chi")
print(by_name.iloc[0]["score"])        # 8.5   (by position 0, i.e. the row "An")
```

### 4. Filtering rows by condition

```python
pass_list = df[df["score"] >= 7.5]
print(len(pass_list))                 # 3
print(pass_list["name"].tolist())     # ['An', 'Chi', 'Em']

# multiple conditions: use & (and), | (or), and put each condition in parentheses
print(df[(df["major"] == "IT") & (df["score"] > 7)]["name"].tolist())   # ['An', 'Em']
```

### 5. Adding columns, sorting, statistics

```python
df["bonus"] = df["score"] + 0.5       # new column, computed row by row
print(df["score"].mean())             # 7.7
top = df.sort_values("score", ascending=False)
print(top.iloc[0]["name"])            # Chi  (highest score)
```

### Common mistakes

- Confusing `loc` (label) with `iloc` (position), especially when the row labels are also numbers.
- Using `and`/`or` instead of `&`/`|` when filtering on multiple conditions.
- Forgetting that `df["a"]` is a Series while `df[["a"]]` is a DataFrame.

### Key takeaways

- DataFrame = table; each column is a Series.
- Use `df.shape`, `df.info()` and `df.describe()` to get familiar with new data.
- `loc` is by label (end included), `iloc` is by position (end excluded).
- Filtering: `df[condition]`; for multiple conditions use `&`, `|` and parentheses.

### Reference

McKinney, W. (2022). *Python for Data Analysis: Data Wrangling with Pandas, NumPy, and Jupyter* (3rd ed.). O'Reilly Media.

## Data Cleaning and Transformation

**After this lesson you will be able to:** detect and handle missing values, duplicate rows, wrong data types and messy strings — the tasks that take up most of the time in a real data project.

### 1. Missing values

Pandas records an empty cell as `NaN`. First, **count** them:

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([8.0, None, 6.0, None, 10.0])
print(s.isna().sum())      # 2   (True counts as 1)
print(s.isna().tolist())   # [False, True, False, True, False]
```

There are two main ways to handle them:

```python
print(s.dropna().tolist())              # [8.0, 6.0, 10.0]      ← drop the missing values
print(s.fillna(s.mean()).tolist())      # [8.0, 8.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0]  ← fill with the mean
```

Which one to choose depends on the problem: dropping rows loses data; filling with the mean keeps the number of rows but makes the distribution "flatter". When computing statistics, `mean()` **skips NaN** by default rather than treating NaN as 0:

```python
print(s.mean())            # 8.0   ← (8 + 6 + 10) / 3
print(s.fillna(0).mean())  # 4.8   ← filling with 0 drags the mean down
```

### 2. Duplicate rows

```python
d = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 2, 3], "v": ["a", "b", "b", "c"]})
print(d.duplicated().sum())        # 1   (the second row of the duplicate pair)
print(len(d.drop_duplicates()))    # 3   (keeps the first occurrence)
```

### 3. Wrong data types

A numeric column that was read as text (because of stray characters) cannot be used in calculations. Use `astype` when you are sure the data is clean, or `to_numeric` when corrupted values may be mixed in:

```python
print(pd.Series(["1", "2", "3"]).astype(int).sum())    # 6

t = pd.to_numeric(pd.Series(["1", "2", "x"]), errors="coerce")
print(t.tolist())    # [1.0, 2.0, nan]  ← "x" cannot be converted, so it becomes NaN
```

`errors="coerce"` turns corrupted values into NaN so you can handle them next with `fillna`/`dropna`.

### 4. Cleaning strings

```python
names = pd.Series([" An ", "BINH"])
print(names.str.strip().str.lower().tolist())   # ['an', 'binh']
```

`.str.strip()` removes whitespace at both ends and `.str.lower()` converts to lowercase. This way `"IT"`, `"it"` and `" IT"` are no longer counted as three different groups when you compute statistics. You can chain several steps together with dots.

To replace specific values: `s.replace("N/A", None)` turns the string `"N/A"` into a missing value.

### Suggested workflow

1. Get an overview: `df.info()`, `df.isna().sum()`, `df.describe()`.
2. Fix data types (`to_numeric`, `astype`).
3. Normalize strings (`.str.strip().str.lower()`).
4. Handle missing values (`dropna` or `fillna`).
5. Remove duplicate rows (`drop_duplicates`).
6. Re-check after each step with `shape` and `isna().sum()`.

### Key takeaways

- Count missing values with `isna().sum()`; `mean()` skips NaN.
- `dropna` removes rows, `fillna` fills in a value.
- `drop_duplicates` keeps the first occurrence.
- `to_numeric(..., errors="coerce")` turns corrupted values into NaN.
- Normalize strings before grouping or counting.

### Reference

McKinney, W. (2022). *Python for Data Analysis: Data Wrangling with Pandas, NumPy, and Jupyter* (3rd ed.). O'Reilly Media.

## Aggregation and Exploratory Data Analysis in Jupyter

**After this lesson you will be able to:** aggregate data by group, read quick summary statistics, and work in a Jupyter Notebook to explore a new dataset.

### 1. Jupyter Notebook in 1 minute

A notebook is made of **cells**: code cells run Python, markdown cells hold notes. The result of the last line in a cell is displayed right below it, which makes notebooks ideal for trying things out and observing data.

- `Shift + Enter`: run the current cell and move to the next one.
- Variables created in one cell can be used in later cells; if you run cells out of order you may get confusing results. When in doubt, choose *Restart Kernel and Run All Cells*.

### 2. Grouping and aggregating: `groupby`

The example dataset:

```python
import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "region":  ["N", "S", "N", "S", "N", "C"],
    "product": ["A", "A", "B", "B", "A", "B"],
    "revenue": [100, 150, 200, 50, 300, 120],
})
```

`groupby` splits the table into groups and then applies an aggregation to each group:

```python
print(sales.groupby("region")["revenue"].sum())
# region
# C    120
# N    600
# S    200

print(sales.groupby("product")["revenue"].mean())
# A    183.333333
# B    123.333333

print(sales.groupby("region").size()["S"])     # 2   (number of rows in group S)
```

Several aggregations at once:

```python
r = sales.groupby("region")["revenue"].agg(["count", "max"])
print(r.loc["N", "count"])   # 3
print(r.loc["N", "max"])     # 300
```

### 3. Quick counts and descriptive statistics

```python
print(sales["region"].value_counts())            # count how often each value appears; N is the most frequent (3)
print(sales["region"].value_counts().idxmax())   # N
print(sales["revenue"].describe())               # count 6, mean 153.33, min, max, quartiles
```

### 4. Cross-tabulation: `pivot_table`

```python
pv = sales.pivot_table(index="region", columns="product",
                       values="revenue", aggfunc="sum")
print(pv)
# product      A      B
# region
# C          NaN  120.0
# N        400.0  200.0
# S        150.0   50.0
```

A cell with no data for that combination (for example, region C has not sold product A) is `NaN`.

### 5. Correlation

```python
xy = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [2, 4, 6, 8], "z": [8, 6, 4, 2]})
print(xy["x"].corr(xy["y"]))   # 1.0   (both increase)
print(xy["x"].corr(xy["z"]))   # -1.0  (when x increases, z decreases)
```

The correlation coefficient lies between −1 and 1: close to 1 means the variables move in the same direction, close to −1 means opposite directions, and close to 0 means little linear relationship. **Correlation does not prove causation.**

### 6. Quick plotting

`sales.groupby("region")["revenue"].sum().plot(kind="bar")` draws a bar chart right in the notebook (you need to install `matplotlib`).

### Workflow for exploring a new dataset

1. `df.shape`, `df.head()`, `df.info()`: what does the data contain?
2. `df.isna().sum()`: where are values missing?
3. `df.describe()` and `value_counts()`: what does the distribution look like, and are there odd values?
4. `groupby` / `pivot_table`: compare between groups.
5. `corr()` and charts: how are the variables related?

### Key Points

- `groupby(column)[numeric_column].aggregation()` is the most commonly used pattern.
- `value_counts()` to count, `describe()` to summarize.
- `pivot_table` for cross-tabulations; a cell with no data is `NaN`.
- Correlation measures how much variables move together, not what causes what.

### Reference

McKinney, W. (2022). *Python for Data Analysis: Data Wrangling with Pandas, NumPy, and Jupyter* (3rd ed.). O'Reilly Media.

items.body:
## Retrieving Data via RESTful APIs

**After this lesson you will be able to:** understand how an API returns data, call an API with the `requests` library, and read JSON data into Python structures.

### 1. What is an API

An **API (Application Programming Interface)** is the doorway through which your program asks another service for data. A **REST API** uses the HTTP protocol: you send a *request* to an address (URL) and receive a *response*, usually in **JSON** format.

The two most important HTTP methods:

| Method | Used to | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | **Retrieve** data without changing anything on the server | Get a list of users |
| `POST` | **Send** data to create something new | Create a post |

### 2. Status codes

A response always comes with a code that tells you the outcome:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `200` | OK — success |
| `401` | Unauthorized — missing or invalid API key/credentials |
| `404` | Not Found — the address or resource does not exist |
| `429` | Too Many Requests — you are calling too fast and are being rate-limited |
| `500` | Internal Server Error — a server-side error |

The `2xx` group means success, `4xx` means an error on the caller's side, and `5xx` means an error on the server's side.

### 3. Calling an API with `requests`

```python
import requests

resp = requests.get(
    "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users",
    params={"_limit": 3},   # query parameters, appended to the URL as ?_limit=3
    timeout=10,             # ALWAYS set a timeout
)
resp.raise_for_status()     # raise an error for 4xx/5xx codes
users = resp.json()         # convert JSON to a Python list/dict
print(resp.status_code)     # 200
print(users[0]["name"])
```

Two important points:

- **`timeout`**: `requests` does not set a time limit by itself, so without this parameter your program can hang forever when the server does not respond.
- **`params`**: let the library encode the parameters and attach them to the URL instead of concatenating strings yourself.

You can see the final URL without making a network call:

```python
req = requests.Request("GET", "https://api.example.com/search",
                       params={"q": "python", "page": 2}).prepare()
print(req.url)    # https://api.example.com/search?q=python&page=2
```

### 4. JSON and Python structures

JSON has two main structures: an **object** `{...}` corresponds to a `dict` and an **array** `[...]` corresponds to a `list`. So you can access them with the familiar indexes and keys:

```python
import json

text = '{"user": {"id": 7, "name": "An", "tags": ["ml", "py"]}, "active": true}'
data = json.loads(text)                 # JSON string → dict
print(type(data).__name__)              # dict
print(data["user"]["tags"][1])          # py
print(data["active"])                   # True   (JSON true → Python True)
print(json.dumps({"a": 1}))             # {"a": 1}   (Python → JSON string)
```

With `requests`, `resp.json()` does exactly what `json.loads(resp.text)` does.

### 5. Good habits when using APIs

- Read the API documentation: the address, parameters, rate limits, and whether an **API key** is needed. Never put a key in publicly shared code.
- Handle errors and set a `timeout`; slow down when you get a `429`.
- Large datasets are usually split into pages (*pagination*): call the pages one by one using parameters such as `page` or `_limit`/`_start`.
- Turn the results into a table for analysis: `pd.DataFrame(users)`.

### Key Points

- `GET` to retrieve, `POST` to send; `2xx` codes mean success, `4xx` a caller-side error, `5xx` a server error.
- Always set a `timeout`; use `params` instead of concatenating strings.
- `resp.json()` returns a `dict`/`list`; JSON object ↔ `dict`, JSON array ↔ `list`.

## Web Scraping with BeautifulSoup **After this lesson you will:** read the structure of an HTML page, use BeautifulSoup to extract data from it, and know when you should (or should not) scrape. ### 1. What scraping is and when to use it **Web scraping** means automatically pulling data out of web pages that are written for human readers. Prefer an **API** whenever the service offers one, because an API is more stable and follows the rules more closely. Scrape only when there is no API and collecting the data is allowed. ### 2. HTML in one minute A web page is made of nested **tags**. Each tag can have attributes such as `class`, `id`, `href`: ```html
  • Pen 3.5
``` ### 3. Parsing HTML with BeautifulSoup The example below uses a ready-made piece of HTML, so you can run it immediately without a network connection: ```python from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """

Shop

  • Pen 3.5
  • Book 12
  • Bag 20
""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") print(soup.h1.text) # Shop print(len(soup.find_all("li"))) # 3 (every li tag) print(soup.find("a")["href"]) # /p/1 (first a tag, read its href attribute) print(soup.find_all("a")[1].get("href")) # /p/2 print(soup.find("table")) # None (find returns None when nothing matches) ``` - `find(...)` returns the **first** matching element (or `None`); `find_all(...)` returns a **list** of all matching elements. - `.text` gets the text inside; `["href"]` or `.get("href")` gets an attribute value. `.get` returns `None` instead of raising an error when the attribute is missing. ### 4. CSS selectors: `select` and `select_one` The syntax is the same as CSS: `tag_name.class`, `#id`, and a space to select a child tag. ```python print(len(soup.select("li.item"))) # 3 print(len(soup.select("li.sale"))) # 1 (only the item that also has class sale) print(soup.select_one("li.sale a").text) # Bag prices = [float(p.text) for p in soup.select("span.price")] print(prices) # [3.5, 12.0, 20.0] print(sum(prices)) # 35.5 ``` Note: `
  • ` has **two** classes, so it matches both `li.item` and `li.sale`. Extracted text is always a string, so you need `float()`/`int()` to do calculations. ### 5. With a real page ```python import requests resp = requests.get("https://books.toscrape.com/", timeout=10) soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, "html.parser") titles = [a["title"] for a in soup.select("article.product_pod h3 a")] ``` The site `books.toscrape.com` was built specifically for practicing scraping. Use it, and do not practice on other people's sites. ### 6. Scraping responsibly - Check `robots.txt` (for example `https://domain-name/robots.txt`) and the site's **terms of use** before collecting data. - Do not fire too many requests in quick succession: wait between calls (`time.sleep`) so you do not overload the server. - A page that **loads its data with JavaScript** after opening will not have that data in the HTML that `requests` receives. In that case, look for the hidden API the page calls, or use a browser automation tool. - Do not collect personal data or data that you are forbidden to collect. ### Key takeaways - `find` gives the first element, `find_all` gives a list; `select`/`select_one` use CSS selectors. - Text and attributes are always strings; convert the type before calculating. - Prefer an API; check `robots.txt` and the terms of use; wait between calls. ### Reference Mitchell, R. (2018). *Web Scraping with Python: Collecting Data from the Modern Web* (2nd ed.). O'Reilly Media.

assignments.title: Module 3 Lab: Collecting Data from APIs and Web Pages
assignments.description:
Collect data from two public sources intended for practice, then turn it into tables for analysis.

**Part A — Get data from an API**

Use `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com` (a sample API, no key needed).

1. Call `GET /users` with `requests`, using `timeout` and `raise_for_status()`. Print `status_code`.
2. Convert the JSON result into a DataFrame, keeping only the columns `id`, `name`, `username`, `email` (plus the city name taken from `address.city`).
3. Call `GET /posts` with `params={"userId": 1}` and count the posts written by user 1.
4. Try calling an address that does not exist (for example `/does-not-exist`) and record the `status_code` you receive together with its meaning.

**Part B — Scrape a real page**

Use `https://books.toscrape.com/` (a site built specifically for practicing scraping).

1. Download the first page with `requests` (with `timeout`) and parse it with BeautifulSoup.
2. Extract the **title** and **price** of the 20 books on the page. Note: if a garbled extra character (mojibake) appears in front of the pound sign in the price, set `resp.encoding = "utf-8"` before reading `resp.text`. Convert the price to a number (`float`).
3. Create a DataFrame `books` with two columns `title`, `price`; compute the average price and print the most expensive book.
4. Fetch a second page (`https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-2.html`), **waiting at least 1 second between the two calls** (`time.sleep(1)`), then combine the two pages with `pd.concat`.

**Part C — Short answers (3–5 sentences)**

- When do you choose an API over scraping, and vice versa?
- What must you check before scraping any page?
- What happens if you forget `timeout`?

**Submit** a `.ipynb` notebook (already run) or a `.py` file together with a screenshot of the results. Do not submit API keys or login credentials.

Grading is based on: calling the API/scraping correctly (with `timeout`, error handling, waiting between calls), correct tabular output, and well-reasoned answers in Part C.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

print(10 // 3, 10 % 3, 2 ** 3)
