What does the following code print?

x = [1, 2, 3]
y = x.copy()
y.append(4)
print(x)
questions.explanation: copy() creates a new, independent list, so appending 4 to y does not affect x: [1, 2, 3].

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

for i in range(3):
    if i == 1:
        continue
    print(i)
questions.explanation: continue skips the iteration where i = 1, so only 0 and 2 are printed.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

def s(*n):
    return sum(n)

print(s(1, 2, 3))
questions.explanation: *n collects the arguments into the tuple (1, 2, 3); their sum is 6.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

class C:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
    def double(self):
        return self.v * 2

print(C(4).double())
questions.explanation: C(4) creates an object with v = 4; double() returns self.v * 2 = 8.

import numpy as np

print(np.arange(1, 6).mean())
questions.explanation: np.arange(1, 6) is [1 2 3 4 5] (it stops before 6); the mean = 15 / 5 = 3.0.

import numpy as np

print(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]).sum(axis=1))
questions.explanation: axis=1 sums along each row: [1 + 2, 3 + 4] = [3 7]. It is axis=0 that gives the column sums [4 6].

print(pd.Series([1, None, 3]).mean())

What does the code print?
questions.explanation: mean() skips missing values: (1 + 3) / 2 = 2.0. Treating the missing value as 0 would give 1.33, but pandas does not do that.

import pandas as pd

d = pd.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "a", "b"], "v": [1, 3, 5]})
print(d.groupby("g")["v"].sum()["a"])

misconceptions.name: Thinking li.item only matches elements with exactly one class
misconceptions.description: The learner believes the li.item selector skips elements that have additional classes, when in fact an element with several classes matches each of its classes.

misconceptions.name: Confusing find with find_all
misconceptions.description: The learner believes find returns an empty list when nothing is found, when in fact find returns None and only find_all returns a list.

misconceptions.name: Confusing GET with POST
misconceptions.description: The learner confuses GET (retrieves data without changing state) with POST (sends data to create something new).

misconceptions.name: Confusing HTTP status code classes
misconceptions.description: The learner confuses client-side errors (4xx, such as 404) with server-side errors (5xx).

misconceptions.name: Confusing axis=0 with axis=1
misconceptions.description: The learner swaps the two axes: axis=0 aggregates across rows (giving a result per column), while axis=1 aggregates across columns (giving a result per row).

misconceptions.name: Thinking * on a list multiplies each element
misconceptions.description: The learner confuses a Python list with a NumPy array: with a list, * repeats the list; only a NumPy array multiplies element by element.

misconceptions.name: Confusing loc (label) with iloc (position)
misconceptions.description: The learner mixes up loc and iloc, forgetting that loc works by label and its slices include the end point, while iloc works by position and excludes the end point.

misconceptions.name: Thinking mean() counts NaN as 0
misconceptions.description: The learner believes missing values are counted as 0 when computing a mean, when in fact pandas skips NaN by default.

misconceptions.name: Confusing Series with DataFrame when selecting columns
misconceptions.description: The learner does not distinguish df['a'] (a Series) from df[['a']] (a DataFrame).

misconceptions.name: Confusing & with | when combining filter conditions
misconceptions.description: The learner confuses '&' (both conditions must hold) with '|' (at least one condition must hold) when filtering a DataFrame.

misconceptions.name: Confusing append with extend
misconceptions.description: The learner confuses append (adds exactly one element, which may itself be a list) with extend (adds each element of an iterable).

misconceptions.name: Thinking .get() raises KeyError for a missing attribute
misconceptions.description: The learner believes tag.get('href') raises an error for a missing attribute the way tag['href'] does, when in fact .get returns None.

misconceptions.name: Thinking BeautifulSoup's .text is a number
misconceptions.description: The learner believes text obtained with .text is automatically a number that can be multiplied, forgetting that it is always a string and needs float()/int().

misconceptions.name: Thinking an object keeps its own copy of a class attribute
misconceptions.description: The learner believes objects created earlier keep the old value of a class attribute after it is changed, when in fact all objects read it from the class.

misconceptions.name: Treating near-zero correlation as independence
misconceptions.description: The learner believes a correlation coefficient near 0 means there is no relationship, forgetting that it only measures linear relationships.

misconceptions.name: Confusing # (id) with . (class) in CSS selectors
misconceptions.description: The learner uses li#sale to select by class, forgetting that # is for id and . is for class.

misconceptions.name: Thinking dropna only drops rows that are missing in every column
misconceptions.description: The learner believes dropna() only drops rows in which all columns are missing, when by default it drops rows with at least one missing value.

misconceptions.name: Thinking a leading __ in an attribute name has no effect
misconceptions.description: The learner believes an attribute starting with two underscores can still be accessed directly from outside the class like a regular attribute.

misconceptions.name: Skipping the data overview step
misconceptions.description: The learner jumps straight into processing or deeper analysis (filling missing values, plotting correlations, groupby) before looking at shape, head, and info.

misconceptions.name: Forgetting the f before an f-string
misconceptions.description: The learner writes {variable} in a regular string and expects Python to substitute the value; without the f prefix the string is printed literally.

misconceptions.name: Using inheritance for a 'has-a' relationship
misconceptions.description: The learner uses inheritance when two classes are only in a containment or ownership (has-a) relationship, instead of an 'is-a' relationship.

misconceptions.name: Treating consecutive ifs as an if/elif chain
misconceptions.description: The learner believes that once one if is true the later ifs are no longer evaluated, when in fact every independent if is checked; only elif/else are skipped.

misconceptions.name: Thinking json.loads keeps JSON's true/null as they are
misconceptions.description: The learner thinks a boolean value after json.loads is still written in lowercase true as in JSON, when in fact Python uses True.

misconceptions.name: Confusing linspace with arange
misconceptions.description: The learner confuses linspace (takes a number of points and includes both endpoints) with arange (takes a step size and stops before the end point).

misconceptions.name: Forgetting self. when assigning attributes in __init__
misconceptions.description: The learner writes name = name in __init__ and expects it to create an object attribute, when it is only a local variable.

misconceptions.name: Thinking the string 'N/A' is already a missing value
misconceptions.description: The learner believes fillna can handle the string 'N/A', when 'N/A' is just an ordinary string until it is converted to NaN.

misconceptions.name: Handling a 429 error by calling even more aggressively
misconceptions.description: The learner responds to a rate-limit error (429) by making more calls instead of slowing down.

misconceptions.name: Thinking self must be passed when creating an object
misconceptions.description: The learner believes the call Student('An') is missing self, forgetting that Python automatically passes the new object into the self parameter.

misconceptions.name: Thinking a set can be indexed like a list
misconceptions.description: The learner accesses a set element by index s[0], forgetting that a set is unordered and therefore does not support indexing.

misconceptions.name: Thinking individual characters of a string can be assigned
misconceptions.description: The learner writes s[0] = 'H' to change a character, forgetting that strings are immutable and a new string must be created.

misconceptions.name: Judging truthiness by the elements inside instead of emptiness
misconceptions.description: The learner believes a list or string containing the value 0 (or False) is falsy, when only an empty container is falsy.

misconceptions.name: Confusing inheritance with polymorphism
misconceptions.description: The learner confuses a subclass reusing its parent's code (inheritance) with the same method name behaving differently depending on the object (polymorphism).

misconceptions.name: Thinking input() returns a number
misconceptions.description: The learner believes input() automatically recognizes numbers and returns an int/float, forgetting that it always returns a string and so needs type conversion.

misconceptions.name: Thinking one object's attribute affects all objects
misconceptions.description: The learner confuses an instance attribute (separate for each object) with a class attribute (shared).

misconceptions.name: Thinking int() rounds a float
misconceptions.description: The learner believes int(3.99) gives 4, when int() truncates the decimal part.

misconceptions.name: Using `is` to compare values
misconceptions.description: The learner uses `is` instead of `==` to compare values, when `is` checks whether two names refer to the same object.

misconceptions.name: Thinking b = a makes a copy of a list
misconceptions.description: The learner believes assigning a list to another variable copies its contents, so changing b does not affect a.

misconceptions.name: Thinking assignment inside a function changes the outer variable
misconceptions.description: The learner believes x = 99 inside a function changes the global variable x, forgetting that the assignment creates a new local variable.

misconceptions.name: Thinking range(a, b) includes b
misconceptions.description: The learner thinks range(2, 6) ends at 6, when it stops just before 6.

misconceptions.name: Thinking the last index of a slice is included
misconceptions.description: The learner reads s[a:b] as including position b, when the slice stops just before b.

misconceptions.name: Confusing / division with // floor division
misconceptions.description: The learner confuses '/' (always returns a float) with '//' (rounds down), or forgets that '%' gives the remainder.

misconceptions.name: Ignoring robots.txt and terms of use when scraping
misconceptions.description: The learner treats being able to fetch the HTML as enough to collect data, without checking the site's robots.txt and terms of use.
